explanations: luna: The same root’s covenant sense appears in the breaking of God’s bond after its confirmation; unlike 89:26’s unmatchable binding, this verse pictures humanly severed ties and corruption. | terra: Those who break God’s مِيثَاق after it has been bound and cut what He ordered joined turn secure moral attachment into rupture, a meaningful abstract counterpart to material وَثَاق.

luna: This account names Pharaoh’s “evil torment” (سُوءَ الْعَذَابِ) and specifies the slaughter of sons; it shows the earthly violence behind the section’s Pharaoh and his claim to punish. | terra: Pharaoh’s people subject the Israelites to سُوءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ by slaughtering sons and sparing women, showing عذاب as a human tyrant’s inflicted violence before the divine reversal.
terra: God takes Israel’s مِيثَاق, raises the Mount above them, and commands them to hold firmly to what they were given; covenantal binding, firmness, and an overhead mass converge in this verse.

terra: The covenant taken from Israel explicitly includes kindness to orphans and the needy, linking the root’s moral bond to the very duty toward the poor whose neglect the section connects to punitive chains.
terra: The covenant-and-raised-Mount scene is repeated, again coupling مِيثَاق with a vast object held above the addressees and a command to take revelation firmly.

luna: Righteousness here includes giving beloved wealth to the needy and freeing those in bondage; these acts reverse both the section’s neglect of the poor and its image of binding. | terra: True righteousness includes giving wealth to the needy and freeing people from bondage, placing the two positive acts opposite the section’s paired neglect of the poor and punitive chaining.

luna: The section’s named root و ث ق appears in the “most trustworthy handhold” (الْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ); here a secure bond is freely grasped and cannot break, a positive counterpart to coercive binding. | terra: ٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ is the secure handhold that never breaks, using the section’s و ث ق root for a saving attachment rather than a punitive bond.
terra: Believers are commanded to hold together to God’s rope, giving a rope the saving and unifying function opposite to the punitive cords and chains developed in the section.
terra: Those who hoard God’s bounty will be collared on Resurrection with what they withheld, directly joining miserliness to a neck-bound punishment as the section joins neglected feeding to chains.
terra: Marriage is called مِّيثَاقًا غَلِيظًا, a weighty covenant; the same root moves firmness from a physical restraint to a solemn interpersonal bond.

luna: The condemned repeatedly receive new skins so they can taste torment; alongside the section’s dictionary account of braided leather entering skin, this makes the body’s surface a site of recurring pain. | terra: Every time the condemned persons’ skins are burned, they receive new skins so that they continue to taste ٱلْعَذَابَ; punishment’s repeated penetration of skin closely fits the section’s etymological image of the whip mixing into hide.

terra: The Mount is raised above Israel because of their covenant, and the verse closes by saying God took from them a solemn covenant; it concretely joins overhead force to the و ث ق root’s moral sense.

luna: The section’s named root و ث ق appears in the covenant with which God “bound” the people (وَاثَقَكُم بِهِ); this is a pledged bond rather than a shackle, clarifying the root’s nonphysical sense beside 89:26. | terra: God tells believers to remember the covenant وَاثَقَكُم بِهِ, using the same و ث ق root for a binding moral commitment and thus developing the section’s secondary sense “to make firm.”

luna: For those who wage war and spread corruption in the land, this ayah names crucifixion among the penalties; it recalls Pharaoh’s crucifixion threat while placing earthly coercion under a divine boundary and judgment. | terra: Crucifixion and opposite-side amputation appear here as a delimited judicial penalty for violent public crime, setting a legal boundary around the same acts Pharaoh threatens arbitrarily in 7:124 and 20:71.

terra: A claim that God’s hand is fettered is answered by saying the speakers’ own hands are fettered; this rhetorical reversal specifically turns an attempted limitation of divine power back upon human beings.

terra: Expiation for a broken oath includes feeding ten needy people or freeing a person from bondage, placing feeding and release together as a precise restorative opposite to neglect followed by binding.

luna: God is said to be able to send punishment from above or below, or make people taste one another’s violence; the vertical descent and multiple forms concretize the section’s “mixed kinds” and mass-from-above image. | terra: God is able to send punishment from above or from beneath people’s feet; the first alternative directly frames divine punishment as the overhead mass that the section finds in فَصَبَّ.
terra: وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهِم مَّطَرًا makes destruction literally descend as rain, the concrete punitive downpour behind the section’s claim that “poured” enlarges a whip into a falling mass.

luna: Pharaoh threatens Moses’ believing magicians with amputation and crucifixion, a repeated human attempt to fasten bodies in punishment against the section’s divine counter-binding. | terra: Pharaoh threatens the magicians with opposite-side amputation and crucifixion, a parallel formulation of the bodily fastening power condensed in his “stakes.”

luna: After Pharaoh threatens crucifixion in 7:124, the magicians say they will return to their Lord; their answer sets the tyrant’s bodily threat against the judgment beyond his control. | terra: After Pharaoh’s parallel threat in 7:124, the magicians answer that they are returning to their Lord, again setting divine destination beyond the reach of his bodily punishment.

luna: The magicians identify their belief as the reason Pharaoh punishes them and ask God for patience and a faithful end; their allegiance makes his torture a temporary coercion rather than ultimate authority.
terra: God takes retribution from Pharaoh’s people and drowns them for denying the signs, another explicit formulation of the tyrant’s final reversal.

luna: The reminder of Pharaoh’s “evil torment” and killing of sons repeats the concrete violence behind the peg-owner’s coercive power. | terra: The same rescue memory calls Pharaoh’s slaughter and oppression سُوءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ, directly giving the “punishment” that the possessor of stakes exercised on bodies.

luna: The Prophet is said to remove the burdens and shackles that were upon people; this is a release from restraint, reversing the punishment binding in the section, though the verse’s shackles are figurative religious burdens. | terra: The Messenger removes people’s burdens and the shackles that were upon them; release from binding supplies the saving opposite to the section’s final, punitive restraint.
terra: The angels are commanded to strike above the necks and every fingertip, giving a literal punitive beating to the dictionary claim that عذاب begins from striking.
terra: The rejecters challenge God to rain stones from the sky or bring painful punishment, explicitly placing a punitive stone-rain and عذاب as parallel demanded outcomes.

luna: At death, angels strike the disbelievers’ faces and backs and tell them to taste the punishment of the Burning Fire; this joins the section’s dictionary account of ع ذ ب as striking to an explicit punishment scene. | terra: Angels strike the faces and backs of the dying disbelievers while telling them to taste burning punishment, directly joining ضرب to عذاب as the section’s dictionary account does.

terra: Pharaoh’s people are cited as a people God seized for their sins, followed by the verdict that God is powerful and severe in punishment; this directly reverses Pharaoh’s boast of superior punitive force.
luna: The section links 69:34 to 89:18’s failure to urge food for the poor; here hoarding gold and silver without spending in God’s way is likewise tied to painful punishment.

luna: The next ayah turns hoarded gold and silver into heated metal that brands foreheads, sides, and backs; this joins the section’s social indictment to a concrete bodily punishment. | terra: Hoarded wealth is heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs; this specifically joins greed to punishment impressed on the body’s surface, where the section locates the whip’s force.

luna: In Lot’s punishment, stones of baked clay are rained down on the town; this is a literal falling mass that clarifies the section’s image of punishment poured from above, though the falling material is stone rather than a whip. | terra: Stones of baked clay are rained upon Lot’s town, giving punishment the overhead weight and multiplicity that the section hears in فَصَبَّ.
terra: Joseph foretells that one prisoner will be crucified and birds will eat from his head; it is a separate, non-Pharaonic crucifixion scene that clarifies the bodily act behind Pharaoh’s threat.
terra: Jacob requires his sons to give a binding pledge from God before entrusting Benjamin to them, using the و ث ق root for a moral surety meant to secure a person’s return.
terra: The eldest brother recalls the binding pledge their father took from them in 12:66, repeating the root’s nonmaterial sense when that pledged security has failed.

luna: Those who deny resurrection are pictured with shackles around their necks and as inhabitants of the Fire; the verse connects rejection to the same bodily restraint and afterlife punishment. | terra: Those who deny resurrection are described with iron collars on their necks and as companions of the Fire, another direct eschatological binding scene.
terra: Those who fulfill God’s covenant and do not break the مِيثَاق preserve a moral bond, showing the constructive form of the firmness that becomes punitive restraint in the section.

luna: This repeats the confirmed covenant’s breaking and severed relations; the section’s root و ث ق can name a social bond people rupture, a contrast to the final binding no one can match. | terra: Those who break God’s covenant after its binding and sever commanded ties repeat the concrete actions of undoing and cutting a bond in an ethical register.
terra: The verse says the punishment of the afterlife is more arduous than punishment in this life and that no one shields from God, a direct scale for the section’s human-versus-divine comparison.

luna: Moses tells his people to recall Pharaoh’s “evil torment,” including slaughtering sons and sparing women; this supplies another Quranic account of the human rule that the section contrasts with God’s punishment. | terra: Moses recalls Pharaoh’s people afflicting Israel with سُوءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ through slaughter, another direct scene of the tyrant’s earthly claim to punish.

luna: The criminals on that day are bound together in shackles (مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي الْأَصْفَادِ), a direct afterlife picture of the binding named in 89:26. | terra: The criminals appear مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي ٱلْأَصْفَادِ, coupled together in fetters, which is the collective chain scene named in the section.

luna: After the criminals bound in chains in 14:49, their clothing is pitch and fire covers their faces; this adds a material bodily torment to that restraint scene. | terra: The criminals bound in fetters in 14:49 wear garments of pitch while fire covers their faces; this verse supplies the bodily punishment into which the preceding restraint delivers them.

luna: This parallel account says stones of baked clay were rained upon Lot’s people; it repeats the specific image of a punitive mass descending from above that the section draws from “poured.” | terra: The overturned town is rained upon with stones of baked clay, another direct staging of punishment as a mass descending from above.
terra: God casts firm mountains into the earth so that it will not sway with people; this is a direct nonlexical parallel to the section’s stake as something driven into ground to hold it steady.
terra: Animal hides are made into light, portable dwellings, using the same hide material that the section says is braided into a whip for shelter rather than bodily punishment.
terra: A woman who unravels her firmly spun yarn becomes the simile for undoing oaths; the verse joins braided material, achieved firmness, and the deliberate loosening of a moral bond.

luna: The command not to make one’s hand “chained to the neck” (مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ) pictures hoarding as self-restraint; beside the section’s poor-feeding indictment, it shows binding imagery can describe withheld wealth. | terra: The miserly hand is pictured as مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ, chained to the neck; this turns refusal to give into the same bodily shackle that the section associates with failure to feed the poor.
terra: The hearers are warned that God may send a stone-bearing storm upon them, a close repeated formulation of punishment descending with a storm’s volume.

terra: Fire encloses the wrongdoers, and their plea for relief brings a molten liquid that scorches faces; confinement and punitive liquid meet in one ayah as the section joins binding with poured punishment.

terra: Dhu al-Qarnayn says that he will punish the wrongdoer and that God will then punish him عَذَابًا نُّكْرًا; the succession explicitly measures a ruler’s limited punishment against God’s final one.

luna: Dhul-Qarnayn sets iron pieces in a gap and pours molten metal over them to seal a barrier; this is a specific worldly act of fastening and containment, used to protect rather than punish, beside the section’s peg and binding images.
terra: Moses and Aaron are told to demand that Pharaoh release Israel and وَلَا تُعَذِّبْهُمْ, explicitly addressing Pharaoh as the human agent of torment whom the section later sees answered.

luna: The section cites Pharaoh’s threat to crucify the magicians on palm trunks and asks who can inflict the more severe, lasting torment; 89:25–26 answers that no human can match God’s punishment or binding. | terra: Pharaoh threatens to cut and crucify the believing magicians in palm trunks, then boasts that his عَذَاب is harsher and more lasting; this is the exact human claim that the section hears 89:25-26 overturning.

luna: The magicians answer the threat in 20:71 by limiting Pharaoh’s power to “this worldly life”; that boundary clarifies why his promised torture cannot rival the judgment in 89:25–26. | terra: The magicians tell Pharaoh to decree whatever he can, because he can decree only this nearer life; the verse directly limits the earthly punisher whose boast appears in 20:71.

luna: The magicians answer Pharaoh’s claim that his punishment lasts longer (20:71) with “Allah is better and more enduring” (وَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ), directly reversing his measure of authority. | terra: The magicians answer that God is better and more lasting, overturning Pharaoh’s immediately preceding assertion that his own punishment is harsher and more lasting.

luna: The criminal who comes to his Lord has Hell and “neither dies therein nor lives”; in the same passage as Pharaoh’s threat, this makes human, time-bounded torment a poor measure of the lasting punishment in the section. | terra: The criminal who comes to God has Hell, where he neither dies nor lives; it supplies the enduring divine outcome behind Pharaoh’s claim in 20:71 that his own عذاب is more lasting.
terra: وَلَعَذَابُ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ أَشَدُّ وَأَبْقَىٰ gives the Quran’s direct verdict that the afterlife punishment is harsher and more lasting, answering Pharaoh’s exact comparative boast in 20:71.
terra: Firm mountains are placed in the earth specifically so that it will not shake with its inhabitants, repeating the stabilizing work expressed by the section’s stake image.

luna: The same root ص ب ب describes boiling water poured from above the heads of the disbelieving disputants; it makes the section’s poured punishment a specific Quranic scene, not merely a large single blow. | terra: يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمُ ٱلْحَمِيمُ is the other exact scene of punitive liquid poured from above, matching the downward volume that the section finds in فَصَبَّ.

luna: The next ayah says the boiling water melts what is in their bellies and their skins; this completes the bodily effect of the head-pour in 22:19 and echoes the section’s account of the lash entering skin. | terra: The liquid poured in 22:19 melts what is inside them and their skins; this verse supplies the bodily result of the preceding pour and meets the section’s account of the whip entering or mixing with the skin.

luna: The scene then adds iron maces for the punished group; that separate striking instrument gives a concrete counterpart to the section’s dictionary note that torment originally meant a blow. | terra: Iron maces are assigned to them immediately after the poured-liquid scene, bringing together the section’s two components: a descending mass and a striking instrument of punishment.

luna: After the boiling-water pour and iron maces in 22:19–21, those who try to leave the Fire are returned to it; the verse adds that their punishment allows no escape. | terra: Whenever the punished try to leave the anguish described in 22:19-21 they are returned and told to taste burning punishment; the verse contributes inescapability to the pour-and-mace scene.

luna: The prescribed hundred lashes are a literal bodily striking, connecting to the section’s dictionary explanation that the source root ع ذ ب began with striking; the fixed count also contrasts with 89:25’s unmatchable torment. | terra: فَٱجْلِدُوا ... مِا۟ئَةَ جَلْدَةٍ is the Quran’s explicit scene of punishment by lashes; its word for a lash also keeps the blow at the skin, the bodily surface from which the section explains the whip’s name.
luna: This separate offense also receives a measured flogging, eighty lashes; it supplies another bounded human instance of the bodily blow that the section sets beside divine punishment.

luna: People thrown into a narrow place in Hell are described as bound together (مُقَرَّنِينَ); this makes confinement itself part of their punishment, like the section’s unmatchable binding. | terra: The condemned are thrown into a narrow place in Hell مُقَرَّنِينَ, bound together; confinement and binding combine into the eschatological وَثَاق image.
terra: Pharaoh threatens to make Moses one of the imprisoned if he takes another god, an indirect but concrete exercise of the confinement power that the section locates in the stake-holder.

luna: This parallel account adds Pharaoh’s threat to cut hands and feet from opposite sides before crucifying the magicians; it repeats the bodily fixation behind the section’s peg and lash images. | terra: Pharaoh threatens opposite-side amputation and crucifixion and asserts that the magicians will know the result, repeating the coercive boast that 89:25-26 answers.

luna: After the threat in 26:49, the magicians say there is no harm and that they return to their Lord; this gives the same human threat a limit beyond Pharaoh’s reach. | terra: Immediately after Pharaoh’s crucifixion threat in 26:49, the magicians say it causes no harm because they are returning to their Lord; their stance denies the tyrant’s punishment final power.
luna: The magicians hope their Lord will forgive them after Pharaoh’s threat; their final appeal places his punishment beside a divine judgment and mercy he cannot control.
terra: وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهِم مَّطَرًا repeats the punitive-rain formula and then calls it an evil rain for those warned, closely matching the section’s downpour reading.
terra: The people of Shuʿayb are seized by “the punishment of the day of shadow,” locating عذاب in an overhead covering and calling it the punishment of a tremendous day.
terra: The same formula rains a destructive rain on the warned people, independently confirming the Quranic scene of punishment arriving with rain’s volume.
luna: Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the people, oppresses a group, kills their sons, and is called a corrupter; this joins the section’s peg-owner, tyranny, and corruption in one scene.

terra: One compact reckoning assigns different peoples a stone storm, a blast, earth-swallowing, or drowning; it concretely matches the dictionary gloss of a “whip” mixed from multiple kinds of punishment.
luna: On the judgment day, punishment covers people above them and beneath their feet; this gives the section’s poured mass an encompassing, inescapable scene rather than a single point of impact.
terra: The verse again says firm mountains were cast into the earth lest it sway with people, a repeated formulation of fastening the ground through peg-like objects.

luna: This repeats the “most trustworthy handhold” (الْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ) for one who submits to God and does good; the source root’s firmness thus also describes chosen reliance rather than imposed restraint. | terra: The person who submits to God is said to have grasped ٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ; this second “firmest handhold” gives divine firmness a protective direction opposite to shackling.
terra: A nearer punishment is distinguished from the greater punishment, giving the section’s contrast between earthly blows and final punishment an explicit two-level vocabulary.

luna: After the weak blame those who led them astray, God places shackles around the disbelievers’ necks; their coercive earthly relation ends in the judgment binding developed by the section. | terra: God places collars on the necks of the disbelievers and says they are repaid only for their deeds, explicitly presenting restraint as measured recompense.

luna: The neck-shackle image appears here as a figure accompanying the disbelievers’ refusal to believe, not as an afterlife sentence; it shows the same restraint image serving a different function. | terra: Shackles are pictured at the rejecters’ necks up to their chins, making them rigid and unable to lower their heads; although figurative in its immediate warning context, the bodily posture sharpens what binding does.

luna: This repeats the section’s title for Pharaoh, ذُو الْأَوْتَادِ, in a list of earlier peoples who denied messengers, confirming that the epithet belongs to his coercive power and eventual judgment. | terra: Pharaoh is again called ذُو ٱلْأَوْتَادِ, the only other Quranic occurrence of his epithet “possessor of stakes,” so this directly fixes the section’s stake image to him.

luna: After naming Pharaoh among deniers in 38:12, this ayah says each denied the messengers and God’s punishment became due; it completes the peg-owner’s placement among those who meet divine retribution.

terra: Solomon has other rebels coupled in fetters, using almost the same مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي ٱلْأَصْفَادِ as 14:49 in a temporal royal setting and thereby distinguishing delegated human restraint from final divine binding.
terra: Job is told to take a bundle in his hand and strike once without breaking his oath; a gathered striking implement used mercifully and sparingly reverses the section’s vast, poured scourge.
luna: This punishment is boiling water and foul discharge; it gives a specific pairing to the section’s source gloss that the whip points to mixed kinds of torment.

luna: The following ayah adds other punishments of the same kind; it explicitly continues the variety described in 38:57. | terra: After boiling liquid and foul fluid in 38:57, وَءَاخَرُ مِن شَكْلِهِۦٓ أَزْوَاجٌ adds other paired kinds; its own stress on multiple varieties matches the gloss of سَوْطَ عَذَابٍ as mixed forms of punishment.
terra: After worldly disgrace, the punishment of the afterlife is said to be greater, another explicit hierarchy that denies any earthly torment the last word.

luna: Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, then ordered into the severest punishment at the Hour; this directly answers Pharaoh’s claim to lasting torment with his own people’s continuing judgment. | terra: Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire and then ordered into أَشَدَّ ٱلْعَذَابِ, a direct Quranic answer to Pharaoh’s claim to possess the harsher punishment.

luna: This ayah stages shackles around necks and chains while the condemned are dragged, a direct bodily counterpart to the section’s binding image. | terra: Collars around necks and chains by which the condemned are dragged concretize the section’s claim that the final وَثَاق becomes an iron chain.

luna: The chained people of 40:71 are then in boiling water and burned in the Fire; it completes the binding-and-punishment scene with heat. | terra: The people dragged by collars and chains in 40:71 are then taken through boiling water and burned; this verse completes the cited chain’s punitive destination.
terra: After a storm humiliates ʿAd in worldly life, the afterlife punishment is called more humiliating, comparing a mass punishment here with the more decisive one to come.
terra: When Pharaoh’s people provoke divine anger, God exacts retribution and drowns them all, turning the earthly punisher into the object of decisive divine force.
terra: God says He rescued the Israelites from ٱلْعَذَابِ ٱلْمُهِينِ; 44:31 identifies that degrading punishment as coming from Pharaoh, so this verse supplies the tyrant’s human عذاب.

terra: مِن فِرْعَوْنَ identifies Pharaoh as the source of the degrading punishment named in 44:30 and characterizes him as haughty and excessive; its own role is to assign the human torment to the stake-holder.
luna: Before the head-pour in 44:48, the condemned man is seized and dragged to the midst of Hell; this contributes forced bodily helplessness to the same punishment sequence.

luna: The section’s named root ص ب ب appears in the command to pour boiling-water torment over a person’s head (صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ مِنْ عَذَابِ الْحَمِيمِ); this is the clearest parallel to a lash of torment poured down as a mass. | terra: ثُمَّ صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ مِنْ عَذَابِ ٱلْحَمِيمِ combines pouring, punishment, and descent from above, making literal the section’s reading of a “poured” whip as an overhead mass rather than one blow.
luna: After the pour in 44:48, the sufferer is addressed ironically as “mighty, noble” (الْعَزِيزُ الْكَرِيمُ); the reversal makes worldly force and rank sound as hollow as Pharaoh’s threat.
terra: ʿAd mistake the approaching cloud for one that will bring rain, but it is a wind containing painful punishment; the verse makes expected rain and descending عذاب occupy the same visible mass.

luna: This is the section’s exact word وَثَاق in a battle scene: captives are tightly bound, then may be released or ransomed when fighting ends. Its bounded human restraint contrasts with 89:26’s unmatchable binding. | terra: فَشُدُّوا ٱلْوَثَاقَ stages the section’s وَثَاق as a firmly tightened bond; the verse’s later release or ransom also bounds this human wartime restraint against the unmatched final binding of 89:26.

luna: This repeats the angels’ striking of faces and backs when taking souls; it is a parallel bodily blow to the strike behind the section’s whip image, though this verse does not name torment. | terra: Angels taking the condemned while striking their faces and backs repeats the punitive beating scene and stands near 47:4’s material bond.
terra: The visiting angels state that they were sent to release stones of clay upon the transgressors, another specific formulation of punishment arriving as many objects from above.
terra: A stone-bearing gale is sent against Lot’s people, a non-rain formulation of the same many-projectile punishment descending with storm-like force.

terra: Pharaoh’s people deny all the signs and are seized with the seizure of One mighty and fully capable, reversing the tyrant’s claim to superior coercive power without reusing the chain vocabulary.

luna: Criminals are recognized and seized by their forelocks and feet; this is a specific forced bodily restraint parallel to the section’s feet-in-fetters dictionary sense and its unmatchable binding. | terra: The criminals are seized by their forelocks and feet, a concrete bodily restraint that recalls the section’s dictionary image of a foot fixed inside a shackle.

terra: وَمَاءٍ مَّسْكُوبٍ places poured water among the delights of the companions of the right; it preserves the section’s water-versus-whip distinction while reversing punitive pouring into provision.
luna: The people of the left are in scorching wind and boiling water; this is a specific pairing of torments that illuminates the section’s dictionary gloss of mixed kinds of punishment.
luna: The next ayah adds a shade of black smoke to the scorching wind and boiling water in 56:42, extending that mixture of torments.
luna: The smoke’s shade is neither cool nor beneficial; this completes the sequence’s varied but unrelieving punishment.
terra: Freeing a person from bondage is required before a couple resume marital contact after ẓihār; the ayah makes release from a bound neck a restorative act rather than a punishment.
terra: For one unable to complete the preceding stages of expiation, feeding sixty needy people is required; this ayah supplies feeding as the companion restorative act to the release in 58:3.
terra: The hearers are warned that God can send a stone storm upon them, turning the section’s downward punitive mass into a direct divine threat.
terra: After the garden owners’ worldly ruin, the verse states that the afterlife punishment is greater; it generalizes the section’s measure of a present affliction against final عذاب.
luna: This is the left-handed record that identifies the person taken and shackled in 69:30; the row’s own detail is the judgment scene that begins that restraint sequence.

luna: The condemned says his wealth did not avail him; this adds the failure of wealth immediately before the authority-loss and shackling in 69:29–30, against the section’s mention of hoarded wealth and neglect of the poor.
luna: The condemned says his authority has departed; that makes the fall from worldly power explicit before the restraint order in 69:30, a sharp reversal of Pharaoh’s coercive authority.

luna: The section cites the order to seize and shackle the person who received his book in the left hand; this is the first bodily restraint in the punishment sequence continued in 69:31–32. | terra: خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ commands that the condemned person be seized and shackled, directly staging the final binding that the section sets against Pharaoh’s power to fasten people.

luna: Between the taking-and-shackling order in 69:30 and the long chain in 69:32, this ayah orders the person to be roasted in Hell; its own contribution is the fire that joins the restraint sequence. | terra: This verse orders the shackled man of 69:30 into Hellfire before the chain of 69:32; its own contribution is to locate the binding inside divine punishment rather than mere custody.

luna: The section cites this long chain, into which the condemned person is to be put; it makes the binding in 89:26 concrete as an afterlife restraint. | terra: The command to insert him into a chain seventy cubits long turns the section’s abstract “binding” into the immense eschatological chain it explicitly cites.

luna: Immediately before the cited failure to urge food for the poor in 69:34, this gives unbelief in God as another cause of the punishment; it locates social neglect within the wider judgment in that passage.

luna: The section explicitly links this failure to urge feeding the poor with 89:18; here it is named as part of the condemned person’s cause, tying the final restraint to neglect of the needy. | terra: وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ gives failure to urge feeding the poor as a reason for the chained person’s fate, exactly joining 89:18 to the binding scene.
luna: Following the punishment and the failure to feed the poor in 69:34, the condemned receives only foul food; that reverses his withholding of food into his own deprivation.
luna: This specifies that only sinners eat the foul food of 69:36, completing the passage’s link between wrongdoing, neglected feeding, and punishment.
luna: The passage identifies the punishment as a blazing fire; the next verse specifies its bodily effect, making it relevant to the section’s physical image of torment.

luna: The flame strips the skin from the head; this is a direct bodily counterpart to the section’s dictionary description of braided leather entering the skin and to its account of severe pain. | terra: The blaze is described with الشَّوَى, commonly understood as stripping skin or bodily extremities; on that reading it supplies the bodily surface affected by the punishment, while the term’s exact anatomical range makes the link uncertain.
luna: The Fire calls those who turned away; this gives the punishment in 70:15–16 an active, pursuing force rather than a passive location.

luna: The same description identifies those who amassed and hoarded wealth; this brings hoarding into the account of the people pursued by punishment, as in the section’s surrounding verses on wealth and feeding the poor. | terra: The Fire calls the person who amassed and withheld wealth; this verse supplies the hoarding offense behind the skin-stripping blaze described in 70:15-16.

luna: The righteous keep a known share of their wealth for those who ask and those deprived; this directly reverses the section’s rebuke for failing to urge food for the poor. | terra: The righteous recognize an assigned right within their wealth, beginning a direct ethical reversal of the hoarder whom the Fire calls in 70:18.

luna: This specifies the recipients of that share as the asker and deprived person; it completes the charitable contrast to the poor-feeding failure linked by the section. | terra: This verse identifies the claimants to that assigned wealth as the petitioner and the deprived, supplying the needy recipients that complete 70:24’s reversal of withholding.

luna: The section cites the same afterlife inventory: shackles (أَنكَالًا) and blazing fire, a direct parallel to its image of punishment joined to binding. | terra: إِنَّ لَدَيْنَا أَنكَالًا وَجَحِيمًا locates shackles and blaze with God, directly supporting the section’s transfer of binding power from the earthly tyrant to divine judgment.

luna: After the shackles and fire in 73:12, this adds choking food and painful torment; it supplies another bodily form in the passage’s combination of punishments. | terra: Choking food and painful punishment follow the shackles and blaze of 73:12; this ayah contributes further distinct forms to the mixed punitive inventory evoked by the section’s whip.

luna: After saying in 73:15 that a messenger was sent to Pharaoh, this ayah says Pharaoh disobeyed and God seized him with a grievous seizure; it shows the peg-owner’s force ending in God’s stronger grasp. | terra: Pharaoh disobeys the messenger and God seizes him with a ruinous seizure; in the same surah as the shackles of 73:12, this makes the famous earthly captor the object of divine force.
terra: Saqar is described as scorching the skin, another precise instance of punishment working upon the bodily surface through which the section explains the whip.
terra: The people of Saqar confess that they did not feed the poor, independently repeating the section’s concrete link between neglect of the needy and eschatological punishment.

luna: The section cites this pairing of chains, fetters, and blazing fire prepared for disbelievers, another direct Quranic joining of restraint and torment. | terra: Chains, iron collars, and a blaze are prepared together for the disbelievers, exactly the punitive restraint-and-fire complex invoked by the section.

luna: The righteous feed the poor, orphan, and captive (مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا); this reverses the section’s cited failure to urge food even for the poor. | terra: The righteous feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite loving the food; within the same surah as the chains of 76:4, this action supplies the moral opposite of the chained man’s neglect in 69:34.
luna: The next ayah says they feed only for God’s sake, seeking neither reward nor thanks; it contrasts care for the captive and poor with the hoarding condemned in the section’s surrounding verses.
luna: Their reason is fear of a grim day; this joins the feeding contrast in 76:8–9 to the final punishment that the section depicts.
luna: After the feeding and fear in 76:8–10, God protects the righteous from that day’s evil; this contrasts the chained punishment cited from 76:4 with safety on the same day.
luna: The next ayah rewards their patience with a garden and silk clothing, a concrete release from the chains and fire named earlier in the same surah.

luna: The section’s named root و ت د also names mountains as pegs (أَوْتَادًا); this gives the peg image a second Quranic scene, with the grounded mountains rather than a human ruler’s coercive title. | terra: وَٱلْجِبَالَ أَوْتَادًا uses the same “stakes” as stabilizing mountain-pegs; their life-sustaining firmness reverses Pharaoh’s coercive use of fastening power.

luna: In Moses’ encounter with Pharaoh, the boast “I am your most exalted lord” (أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ) frames the same human claim of mastery that the section’s peg-owner embodies; 79:25 supplies the answer.

luna: After Pharaoh’s claim in 79:24, God seizes him with the exemplary punishment of the first and later life; this reverses the section’s Pharaoh’s boast that his own punishment can be strongest and lasting. | terra: God seizes Pharaoh with نَكَالَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ وَٱلْأُولَىٰ, making the tyrant who threatened punishment himself the object of exemplary divine punishment.
terra: God “anchors” the mountains, expressing with a different verb the same fixing-to-earth action that underlies the section’s stake dictionary sense.

luna: The section’s named root ص ب ب also describes God pouring water abundantly; here the action is provision rather than torment, exposing the striking difference between a life-giving pour and 89:13’s punishment. | terra: أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا is the Quran’s exact positive instance of water being poured, confirming the section’s lexical contrast that one pours water while a whip is ordinarily struck.

luna: The next ayah says the earth is split open after the abundant water of 80:25; that is the soil’s response to the same pour, continuing its life-producing contrast to the section’s destructive mass.
luna: Grain grows from the watered earth; this completes the positive result of the same root’s pouring in 80:25, against the section’s poured lash.

luna: After poured water, earth-splitting, and grain in 80:25–27, the passage names grapes and fodder; it continues the beneficial harvest produced by the same root ص ب ب that the section uses for punishment.
luna: The watered growth continues with olives and date palms; this is another concrete provision from the section’s root ص ب ب in its contrasting, life-giving use.
luna: The passage next names dense gardens, continuing the crop scene after the abundant water of 80:25 and contrasting it with a punitive pour.
luna: Fruit and pasture complete the produce list begun after the poured water; the verse continues the same root’s beneficial result.
luna: The passage concludes that the crops are provision for people and livestock; this completes the positive purpose of the pour whose punitive counterpart the section develops.

terra: Those who tortured believing men and women in fire face the punishment of Hell and burning; a human persecutor is thus subjected to the same kind of divine reversal the section sees for Pharaoh.
terra: The person in the greatest Fire neither dies nor lives, a concise description of the endurance implicit in the claim that divine punishment outlasts Pharaoh’s.
terra: فَيُعَذِّبُهُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْعَذَابَ ٱلْأَكْبَرَ names God as agent of “the greatest punishment,” a concise parallel to the unmatched punishment of 89:25.

luna: Freeing a neck (فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ) is the first act named in the steep path; it directly reverses the section’s binding image. | terra: فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ makes freeing a neck the steep saving act, a precise reversal of collars, shackles, and the unbreakable punitive bond in the section.

luna: The next act is feeding people on a day of hunger, a direct reversal of the failure to urge food for the poor cited by the section. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger continues the liberating “steep path” opened by freeing a neck in 90:13, reversing both the section’s bond and its failure to feed.

luna: The steep path includes caring for an orphan of close relation; this complements 90:14’s feeding and reverses the failure to honor the orphan in 89:17, the surrounding context of the section’s poor-feeding link.

luna: The next recipient is a person in misery and need; this specifies whom the feeding path serves, against the neglect condemned around 89:18. | terra: A destitute person is the recipient specified after the feeding act of 90:14; this verse completes that passage’s positive reversal of failing to urge food for the miskīn.
luna: This ayah praises those who urge one another to patience and mercy; it reverses the section’s specific rebuke of those who do not urge care for the needy.
terra: The birds pelt the army with stones of baked clay, staging a collective punitive shower from overhead without using the rain verb.

luna: This ayah repeats the section’s specific phrase about not urging food for the poor (وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ), making the condemned omission a repeated Quranic measure of conduct. | terra: وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ repeats 69:34’s wording almost exactly and therefore reinforces the specific offense that the section connects to the chain.
luna: The closing rebuke says they withhold even small acts of aid; it sharpens the same withholding of care that the section links from 69:34 to 89:18.
terra: A rope of twisted palm fibre around the neck supplies both an organically braided binding material and a punitive neck restraint, close to the section’s woven leather and final bond.
